kurz: How often active funds miss their benchmark, measured in three independent data sets using different methods, and what a critical recalculation changes about this finding.

bloecke.md:
No one disputes that some fund managers beat the market. The open questions are how many manage it, over what periods and whether the successful funds can be identified in advance.

There are three large data sets on this. They come from different providers, measure against different benchmarks and each have their own weaknesses. They are meaningful above all when taken together, because they reach the same result despite these differences.

## Method of the SPIVA scorecards

The [[SPIVA]] scorecards from S&P Dow Jones Indices are published every six months. They measure what proportion of actively managed funds in a category lagged behind the corresponding benchmark. Performance is measured after ongoing charges, but before initial charges, custody fees and taxes.

Three methodological choices shape the result. First, funds that were closed or merged during the period are included and counted as underperformers. Without this correction, only surviving funds would be compared ([[survivorship bias]]). Second, SPIVA counts on an equal-weighted basis, so that a fund with ten billion euros carries as much weight as one with ten million. Third, the benchmark is an index, and an index pays neither a management fee nor spreads and does not have to hold a cash reserve. All three choices make the figures stricter than what an investor experiences. The criticism of SPIVA also targets these same three points.

bloecke.titel: Share of active funds below their benchmark by investment horizon
bloecke.unter: Reference date 30 June 2025. The longer the period, the higher the share. Across all regions, this pattern is the most stable in the entire SPIVA history.

bloecke.md:
Over one year, 74.9% of active US equity funds missed the S&P Composite 1500, over ten years 90.3% and over twenty years 93.8%. If SPIVA also adjusts for the volatility taken on, the twenty-year figure rises to 96.8%. In Europe, 93% of active equity funds lagged their benchmark over ten years, and 80% of bond funds.

Over short periods, the rates fluctuate strongly, and the categories sometimes move in opposite directions. In 2024, 65% of active US large-cap funds lagged the S&P 500, while among US small caps the figure in the same year was only 29.7%, the best value ever measured for this category. A single good year does not refute the long-term figures. It shows how much random fluctuation (noise) there is in short periods.

bloecke.titel: Share of euro-denominated active funds below the benchmark (SPIVA Europe, 30 June 2025)

bloecke.md: The most meaningful figure is in the first row of the table. Global equity funds in euros are the largest active category in Europe and the direct counterpart to the world ETF. Of these, 98.2% missed the S&P World over ten years. Barely one in 56 came out ahead, and which one that would be could not be identified in 2015.

## How the rate rises with the investment horizon

The rise is not due to managers getting worse over the years. Three mechanisms work together.

First, the cost gap acts again every year on capital that has grown in the meantime. Second, a lead has to be maintained in every sub-period, and one weak five-year stretch is enough to wipe it out. Third, the population shrinks. Of the European equity funds that existed ten years earlier, 58% still existed on the reference date. In the US, 37.3% of the funds with a twenty-year history survived. Funds that have performed well are rarely closed.

In May 2026, Cremers, Fulkerson and Riley presented a recalculation of the SPIVA year-end 2024 edition. They weight by assets under management instead of by number of funds. Closed funds are included with the return they achieved up to closure instead of being counted across the board as underperformers. The comparison is made with real index funds that charge fees instead of with the index. This gives, for US equity funds over the twenty years from 2005 to 2024, averaged across twelve categories by size and investment style, around 55% underperformance instead of 92%, and for bond funds over ten years 37% instead of 71%. For bonds, the conclusion is thus reversed. The 92% therefore relates to a different reference date and a different scope from the 93.8% for all US equity funds as of 30 June 2025 mentioned above.

The study was funded by the Active Managers Council of the Investment Adviser Association. SPIVA, in turn, comes from an index provider. Both sets of interests are disclosed, and both methods of calculation can be traced. What needs to be assessed is therefore the methodology, regardless of who produced it.

With the mildest defensible figure, the odds for equity funds are roughly even. The costs of the active funds have already been deducted, because the study compares net returns. Since slightly more than half of the assets in active US equity funds lagged comparable index funds, this calculation also shows no advantage for active funds. For bonds, by contrast, the evidence for a passive approach is considerably weaker.

## Comparison with index funds you can buy

The Morningstar Active/Passive Barometer takes into account the objection that weighs most heavily against SPIVA. It measures active funds against the asset-weighted average of the index funds in the same category, that is, against products an investor can buy, including their costs. A fund counts as a success only if it survives the period and has beaten this average.

Over the ten years to June 2025, 21% of active US strategies achieved this, and around 25% over the ten years to June 2026. For European equity funds, Morningstar reports success rates for the first half of 2026 of 28.4% over one year, 20.3% over three, 15.2% over five and 11.9% over ten years. Even with the fairer benchmark, the order of magnitude does not change.

bloecke.titel: Ten-year success rate of active US funds by category
bloecke.unter: Share of funds that survived the period and beat the cost-adjusted average of the index funds in their category. Source: Morningstar, as of 30 June 2025. No category reaches 53%.

bloecke.md:
The differences between the categories have understandable reasons. The rates are lowest where many analysts follow the same few hundred companies and information is cheap. They are 2.8% for US large growth stocks, 5.8 for US blue chips and 7.0 for global blue chips. They are higher where indices are heterogeneous and difficult to replicate, for example for corporate bonds (52.2%), global real estate funds (51.6), high-yield bonds (43.0) and emerging markets (30.8).

Two caveats apply. Even in the most favourable categories, the success rate is only about half, so the odds are at best even. In addition, the category would have to be chosen in advance, and the ranking of the categories is not stable.

## Costs as a selection criterion

If the same funds are sorted by their ongoing charges, clear differences emerge. Over ten years, 27% of the funds in the cheapest cost quintile did better than their passive counterpart, but only 15% of those in the most expensive quintile (all categories, as of June 2025). For US blue chips, the figures were 15.4% versus 3.9%; in the 2026 edition they are 23% versus 9%. For emerging market funds, this edition gives 52% versus 27%. No other characteristic separates as reliably, neither the star rating nor fund size nor the manager's track record.

This has nothing to do with the managers' talent. The expense ratio is the only one of these characteristics that is fixed in advance. For the EU, ESMA puts the ongoing charges of active equity UCITS over ten years at 1.50% a year, and those of ETFs at 0.31%. Net returns were 9.4% compared with 10.4%. The return gap of 1.0 percentage points was thus of the same order of magnitude as the cost gap of 1.19 percentage points.

In Germany, when funds are sold through banks and intermediaries, there is often an initial charge on top, usually up to 5% of the unit value, which is up to 4.76% of the amount invested. In addition, there is an ongoing trail commission paid out of the management fee. Such inducements are permitted in commission-based advice but must be disclosed under Section 70 WpHG (Securities Trading Act). In fee-based investment advice (Honorar-Anlageberatung), they must be passed on to the client (Section 64(5) WpHG).

The assumptions are a lump-sum investment of €20,000 over twenty years and a market return of 8.5% a year, roughly what the MSCI World achieved net in euros from 1988 to 2025.

- An ETF with ongoing charges of 0.20% returns 8.30% net and reaches a final value of €98,537.
- With an active fund with a 5% initial charge and ongoing charges of 1.50%, €19,048 is invested. That leaves 7.00% net, and the final value is €73,708.

The difference is €24,829, without the manager having made a single mistake. To draw level, the manager would have to earn 10.06% a year gross, that is, 1.56 percentage points more than the market. This applies on average over twenty years; individual outstanding years are not enough. Without the initial charge, 9.80% would be needed. Illustrative calculation before tax.

The U.S. Persistence Scorecard tracks how the top-ranked funds perform in the following years. Of the US equity funds that were in the top quartile of their category in 2021, none of the large-, mid- and multi-cap funds was in the top quartile again in each of the four following years from 2022 to 2025. Among small-cap funds, the figure was around 2%. With pure chance, it would be 0.25 to the power of four, that is, 0.39%.

bloecke.titel: Top funds of 2021 remaining in the top quartile
bloecke.unter: The starting set is the 164 US large-cap funds that were in the top quartile in 2021. As a preselection tool, the ranking thus provides a signal that is weaker than chance.

bloecke.md:
## Predictability of successful funds

There are three reasons, each acting independently of the others, why the successful exceptions cannot be identified in advance.

The first reason is statistical. The annual lead of a good fund is small relative to its fluctuation. That is why even a ten-year track record says little about whether the [[alpha]] is based on skill or on luck. The time series is too short for the dispersion it contains.

The second reason is economic. Berk and Green modelled what happens to a recognisably good fund. It receives inflows until its strategy runs into capacity limits and the excess return disappears. The fund company then earns from the size, and the investor once again receives the market return. Investors who only buy once the skill is visible therefore hardly benefit from it any more.

The third reason is practical. A fund is almost always selected at the end of a good run, because only such funds stand out. Purchases are therefore systematically made after the phase that made the fund attractive.

What can be determined in advance, by contrast, are inconspicuous but stable characteristics such as the expense ratio, initial charge, breadth of the portfolio and turnover.

## Tax differences from the US

In US sources, the tax disadvantage of active funds takes up a lot of space. There, realised capital gains are distributed to investors every year and become taxable immediately, and the more often a fund turns over its holdings, the more expensive this becomes. This cannot be transferred to German investors. Since the 2018 investment tax reform, what is taxed here are the distributions, plus the [[Advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)|advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)]] (Section 18 InvStG, Investment Tax Act) and the gain on sale (Section 16(1) no. 3 in conjunction with Section 19 InvStG, Section 20(1) no. 3 EStG (Income Tax Act)). Trading within the fund is not taxed.

The [[Flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)|flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)]] of 25% plus the solidarity surcharge, together 26.375%, and the [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] of 30% for equity funds (Section 20(1) InvStG; equity participation ratio (Kapitalbeteiligungsquote) of more than 50% under Section 2(6) InvStG) apply equally to active and passive funds. The effective tax burden on the gain is therefore around 18.5%. Taxation thus does not change the ranking.

Tax does play a role elsewhere. Switching from an expensive active fund to an index fund is a sale. If large book gains are realised in the process, the tax is due immediately, and that amount no longer remains invested. This is no argument against switching, though it is an argument for doing the calculation beforehand, for example spreading the switch over several years and making use of the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 (Section 20(9) EStG).

1. Clarify the benchmark against which the return is shown. This can be an index, an index fund of the same category that you can buy, or a self-selected peer group.
2. Check the period and look at what the same figure looked like before the last good phase.
3. Add up ongoing charges, transaction costs, initial charge and trail commission. The annual reduction in return is shown in the key information document.
4. Find out how many funds there were in this category at the start of the period shown and how many of them still exist today.

None of these figures says that successful active management is impossible. They show that the probability of success is low and falls further with the length of the investment period, that success does not persist and that price is the only selection criterion available in advance. The choice between active and passive is thus based on probabilities rather than certainties.

mitnehmen: Over ten years, 90.3% of active US equity funds and 98.2% of euro-denominated global equity funds missed their benchmark, and the rate rises with the investment horizon, regardless of market conditions.
Even in the fairer comparison with real index funds, the ten-year success rate is only 21% to 25% in the US and 11.9% for European equity funds.

Success does not persist: of the top US funds of 2021, apart from small-cap funds, none was in the top quartile again in each of the four following years, whereas pure chance would have produced 0.39%.
Costs are the only characteristic by which funds reliably differ in their probability of success, and the cheapest cost quintile achieves roughly twice the success rate of the most expensive.

The methodological criticism of SPIVA is justified and softens the figures considerably; for bonds, it even reverses the result. For equities, the chance of success after costs remains roughly even, so the recalculation also shows no advantage for active funds.

begriffe.text: Semi-annual analysis by S&P Dow Jones Indices that tracks how many of the funds that were once top-ranked remain in the top quartile in the following years. The benchmark is the chance expectation of 25% a year.

Series of studies by Morningstar that measures active funds against the asset-weighted average of the index funds in the same category instead of against an index. A fund counts as a success only if it survives the period and beats this average.

One-off sales fee charged when buying fund units, in Germany usually up to 5% of the unit value, that is, up to 4.76% of the amount invested. The charge permanently reduces the capital invested and therefore has an effect over the entire investment period.

Ongoing share of the management fee that the fund company pays to the intermediary. The commission is permitted in commission-based advice and must be disclosed (Section 70 WpHG); in fee-based investment advice (Honorar-Anlageberatung), it must be passed on to the client (Section 64(5) WpHG).
